description: We are The Void Voyagers from Calgary, a multidisciplinary team dedicated to tackling theNASA Space Apps Challenge. We are building innovative health-monitoring software to ensure astronaut safety, well-being, and peak performance during long-duration space missions.
summary:
BASELINE is a crew-health console for long missions. A simulated 180-day mission plays in about five minutes for a four-person crew. BASELINE learns each astronaut's own normal from the first 14 days, then watches five signals — heart rate, HRV, temperature, sleep and activity — and flags slow drift before symptoms appear. Every alert explains itself in plain language, lists other possible explanations, prescribes an onboard countermeasure, and re-checks whether the crew member actually recovers.

A second "Earth" tab shows the other half of the problem: distance. Mars Mode puts a 22-minute one-way delay on every message, so reports crawl, arrive stamped with how old the data was, and advice lands late. The ship keeps working while it waits.

It matters because on deep-space missions nobody can call for help in time. Catching a trend days early, and being able to explain why the system flagged it, is the difference between a treated problem and an emergency. Data is simulated; the rules are transparent, not a black box.
details:
1. What does it do and how does it work?

BASELINE is an autonomous crew-health monitoring and early-warning console built for long-duration deep-space transit (such as a 180-day mission to Mars). It operates on a 5-step operational loop: Learn, Watch, Explain, Act, and Re-check.

  • Personal Calibration (Learn): Rather than evaluating astronauts against static, one-size-fits-all Earth population averages, BASELINE spends the mission’s first 14 days learning each individual astronaut’s personal baseline in microgravity.
  • Multi-Signal Drift Detection (Watch): It continuously tracks 5 core physiological signals: resting heart rate, heart rate variability (HRV), core body temperature, daily sleep hours, and physical activity/strain, alongside environmental parameters (such as cabin CO2CO2​levels and cumulative radiation). Rather than waiting for a single vital to spike into an acute emergency, it detects subtle, correlated multi-signal drift over rolling 7-day windows.
  • Explainable Alerts (Explain): When drift occurs, it issues an explainable alert in plain language detailing which signals deviated from baseline, provides a differential cause analysis (e.g., distinguishing infection drift from acute physical fatigue), and flags environmental cross-correlations.
  • Action & Verification (Act & Re-check): Astronauts can initiate structured onboard countermeasures (such as hydration regimens, protected sleep cycles, or biomarker tests) directly on the console. The system continuously re-checks their vitals and confirms recovery back to baseline.
  • Earth Ground Link (#/earth): A synced ground-station console simulates interplanetary speed-of-light radio delay (up to 22 minutes one-way in Mars Mode). The onboard outbox queues, tracks, and visibly crawls transmission packets (STORED →→ SENT →→ RECEIVED →→ CONFIRMED), allowing the ship to act autonomously while Earth advice travels.

2. What benefits does it have?

  • Overcomes Communication Blackouts: On a Mars mission, round-trip communication takes up to 44 minutes. BASELINE allows the crew to identify and address health changes immediately without waiting for Houston.
  • Catches Subclinical Illness Early: Detects early warning signs of infection, dehydration, renal stone risk, and physical fatigue days before clinical symptoms become debilitating.
  • Eliminates "Black Box" Confusion: Built on deterministic, auditable rules rather than hallucination-prone generative models. Non-physician crew members can understand exactly why an alert fired and what steps to take.
  • Low Cognitive Burden: Uses flight-deck grade dark-mode UI with high-contrast semantic alerts and an interactive 3D/SVG clickable body map for intuitive, rapid assessment.

3. What is the intended impact?

The intended impact is to bridge the gap between Earth-dependent spaceflight and interplanetary medical autonomy. By catching health anomalies at the subclinical stage, BASELINE prevents minor issues from escalating into life-threatening emergencies, preserves limited onboard medical resources, reduces astronaut cognitive strain during isolation, and ensures mission success when Earth is out of reach.

4. What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?

  • Frontend Architecture: React 19, TypeScript, and Vite.
  • Styling & Design System: Tailwind CSS with custom semantic design tokens (dark cockpit flight-deck theme), Phosphor Icons, and Geist typography.
  • Data Visualization & Interaction: Recharts for dynamic multi-signal trendlines and rolling baselines; interactive SVG Body Map with clickable physiological regions.
  • Communication & Telemetry Sync: Browser BroadcastChannel API (with localStorage fallback) providing serverless, multi-window synchronization between the Ship Console and the Earth Station view.
  • Testing & Quality Assurance: Native node:test suite covering engine simulation, baseline drift mathematics, outbox packet state machines, and session persistence.
  • Hosting & Deployment: Firebase Hosting and Vercel static deployment targets.
  • Software: Lovable.dev through the development and deployment process.

5. How is your project creative?

  • The Dual-Window Communication Delay Demo: Instead of just talking about communication latency, BASELINE creates an interactive second-tab simulation (#/earth). Judges and users can turn on "Mars Mode" and physically observe telemetry packets queue up and crawl over space, experiencing firsthand why onboard autonomy is mandatory.
  • Holistic Body-to-Signal Mapping: Rather than isolated tables of numbers, astronauts click directly on body zones (cardiovascular, renal, neurological/cranial, musculoskeletal) to reveal correlated vitals and risk profiles.
  • Pre-symptomatic, Multi-Vital Correlation: Moving away from traditional single-threshold beepers toward multi-variate drift detection tailored to personal microgravity baselines.

6. What factors did your team consider?

  • NASA’s Five Hazards of Spaceflight (RIDGE): Specifically incorporated radiation exposure, distance from Earth (latency), isolation/confinement (sleep & behavioral strain), altered gravity (fluid shifts and stone risk), and hostile closed environments (cabin CO2CO2​spikes).
  • Open Science & Real Space Research: Grounded in physiological findings from NASA’s Human Research Program (HRP) and Open Science Data Repository (OSDR), as well as Canadian Space Agency (CSA) radiation and astronaut health research.
  • "Decision Support, Not Diagnosis": Recognizing clear ethical and medical boundaries—the console provides decision support and trend triage for astronauts and flight surgeons, rather than diagnosing clinical disease.
  • Zero-Server Reliability: Long-duration spacecraft cannot depend on cloud servers. The entire engine, drift calculator, and storage run entirely client-side on the device.
